props.title: The Tree of Wooden Clogs
props.initialSlug: Poor farming families struggle in 1890s Lombardy

sections.content: **The Tree of Wooden Clogs** (1978) stands as Ermanno Olmi's masterpiece of Italian neorealism, documenting a year in the lives of four peasant families in late 19th-century Lombardy. Shot with non-professional actors and meticulous attention to historical detail, it shares DNA with De Sica's **Bicycle Thieves** (1948) and Visconti's **La Terra Trema** (1948), but achieves an even more immersive ethnographic quality. The film's 3-hour runtime unfolds like a living museum of agricultural life, capturing everything from grape harvesting to pig slaughtering with documentary precision.

sections.content: What sets Olmi's approach apart is his resistance to melodrama or political messaging. Unlike many neorealist works like **Rome, Open City** (1945) or **Bitter Rice** (1949), The Tree of Wooden Clogs avoids overt commentary on class struggle. Instead, it presents the dignity of labor and religious faith matter-of-factly, as integrated parts of peasant life. The film's central incident - a father chopping down a tree to make his son's clogs for walking to school - becomes powerful precisely because it's presented without dramatic emphasis.

Olmi's use of direct sound and natural light pioneered techniques later seen in films like **The Return** (2003) and **Silent Light** (2007). His influence extends to contemporary social realists like the Dardenne brothers, whose **Rosetta** (1999) and **Two Days, One Night** (2014) share his commitment to unvarnished portrayals of working-class life. sections.content: The film's cinematography transforms mundane agricultural tasks into visual poetry, predating similar approaches in **Le Quattro Volte** (2010) and **Honeyland** (2019). Olmi, who operated his own camera, captures morning mist over the fields and candlelit faces with the same reverential attention he gives to religious processions. This visual strategy influenced later rural-focused films like **Happy as Lazzaro** (2018) and **The Wonders** (2014).
